groups.source: At a constant acceleration of thirty-two feet per second squared, velocity after t seconds is thirty-two t.
groups.caption: At a constant 32 ft/s² from rest, v = 32t in ft/s when t is in seconds.
groups.reason: Keep stated physical units, sign convention, assumptions and worked values legible at narration speed.

groups.source: At two point four seconds it is seventy-six point eight feet per second.
groups.caption: At t = 2.4 s, v = 76.8 ft/s.
groups.reason: Keep stated physical units, sign convention, assumptions and worked values legible at narration speed.

groups.source: An initial velocity v zero adds a rectangle beneath the line.
groups.caption: An initial velocity v₀ adds a rectangle under the line.
groups.reason: Keep stated physical units, sign convention, assumptions and worked values legible at narration speed.

groups.source: Displacement is therefore v zero t plus one half a t squared.
groups.caption: Displacement is Δx = v₀t + ½at².
groups.reason: Keep stated physical units, sign convention, assumptions and worked values legible at narration speed.

groups.source: This version divides by acceleration, so acceleration must be nonzero.
groups.caption: The numerator uses −v₀ and the square root. The denominator is a, so a must be nonzero.
groups.reason: Keep stated physical units, sign convention, assumptions and worked values legible at narration speed.

groups.source: Setting minus seventy-nine point two five plus thirty-two t to zero gives about two point four seven seven seconds.
groups.caption: Solve −79.25 + 32t = 0. The apex is at about 2.477 s.
groups.reason: Keep stated physical units, sign convention, assumptions and worked values legible at narration speed.

groups.source: Returning to the starting height means zero displacement. Factor t out of the position equation to obtain two times: zero, the launch instant, and about four point nine five three seconds.
groups.caption: At the starting height, displacement is 0. Factoring out t gives 0 s at launch and about 4.953 s on return.
groups.reason: Keep stated physical units, sign convention, assumptions and worked values legible at narration speed.

groups.source: Subtract the displacement supplied by the initial velocity, multiply the remaining difference by two, then divide by time squared.
groups.caption: Subtract v₀t from the target displacement. Then a = 2(Δx − v₀t)/t².
groups.reason: Keep stated physical units, sign convention, assumptions and worked values legible at narration speed.

groups.source: To travel fifteen meters in three seconds from two meters per second, the initial velocity contributes six meters. Acceleration must supply the remaining nine, giving two meters per second squared.
groups.caption: To cover 15 m in 3 s from 2 m/s, the initial speed supplies 6 m. Acceleration supplies the remaining 9 m: a = 2 m/s².
groups.reason: Keep stated physical units, sign convention, assumptions and worked values legible at narration speed.

groups.source: The gravity magnitude g is positive, so vertical acceleration is minus g.
groups.caption: Gravity’s magnitude g is positive; vertical acceleration is −g.
groups.reason: Keep stated physical units, sign convention, assumptions and worked values legible at narration speed.

groups.source: From an origin at launch, horizontal position is initial horizontal velocity times t, and height is initial vertical velocity times t minus one half g t squared.
groups.caption: From the launch point, x = v₀ₓt and y = v₀ᵧt − ½gt².
groups.reason: Keep stated physical units, sign convention, assumptions and worked values legible at narration speed.

groups.source: At the apex, vertical velocity is zero, so apex time is initial vertical velocity divided by g.
groups.caption: At the apex, vertical velocity is 0, so the time to the apex is v₀ᵧ/g.
groups.reason: Keep stated physical units, sign convention, assumptions and worked values legible at narration speed.

groups.source: Substituting it into the height equation gives maximum height equal to the square of initial vertical velocity divided by two g.
groups.caption: Substituting that time gives a height gain of v₀ᵧ²/(2g).
groups.reason: Keep stated physical units, sign convention, assumptions and worked values legible at narration speed.

groups.source: For angle theta measured above horizontal and initial speed s zero, the horizontal component is s zero cosine theta and the vertical component is s zero sine theta.
groups.caption: With launch speed s₀ and angle θ above horizontal, the components are s₀ cos θ and s₀ sin θ.
groups.reason: Keep stated physical units, sign convention, assumptions and worked values legible at narration speed.

groups.source: Substitute them into the time and range formulas; using the double-angle identity, same-height range becomes speed squared times sine of twice the angle, divided by g.
groups.caption: Substitute into the range formula and use the double-angle identity. At equal launch and landing heights, range is s₀² sin(2θ)/g.
groups.reason: Keep stated physical units, sign convention, assumptions and worked values legible at narration speed.

groups.source: Dividing it into n equal pieces gives width delta x equal to b minus a over n.
groups.caption: Split the interval into n equal pieces. Each has width Δx = (b − a)/n.
groups.reason: Keep stated physical units, sign convention, assumptions and worked values legible at narration speed.

groups.source: Thus the i-th left endpoint is a plus i minus one times delta x.
groups.caption: The i-th left endpoint is a + (i − 1)Δx.
groups.reason: Keep stated physical units, sign convention, assumptions and worked values legible at narration speed.

groups.source: A constant one hundred watts for two seconds uses two hundred joules; changing power requires accumulating the area under its graph.
groups.caption: At a constant 100 W for 2 s, the energy is 200 J. For varying power, accumulate the area under the graph.
groups.reason: Keep stated physical units, sign convention, assumptions and worked values legible at narration speed.

groups.source: An antiderivative of t squared is t cubed over three; differentiating verifies it.
groups.caption: An antiderivative of t² is t³/3. Differentiating gives t² again.
groups.reason: Keep stated physical units, sign convention, assumptions and worked values legible at narration speed.

groups.source: The exception is exponent minus one, because the new exponent would be zero.
groups.caption: The power rule for integration excludes exponent −1: the new exponent would be 0.
groups.reason: Keep stated physical units, sign convention, assumptions and worked values legible at narration speed.

groups.source: For one over t on a nonzero interval, an antiderivative is the natural logarithm of absolute t.
groups.caption: On an interval where t ≠ 0, an antiderivative of 1/t is ln|t|.
groups.reason: Keep stated physical units, sign convention, assumptions and worked values legible at narration speed.

groups.source: Adding three or ten to t squared gives the same derivative, two t.
groups.caption: Both t² + 3 and t² + 10 have derivative 2t.
groups.reason: Keep stated physical units, sign convention, assumptions and worked values legible at narration speed.

groups.source: Its indefinite integral is therefore a family, t squared plus C, rather than one unique function.
groups.caption: The indefinite integral of 2t is the family t² + C.
groups.reason: Keep stated physical units, sign convention, assumptions and worked values legible at narration speed.

groups.source: If f is continuous on the interval and capital F is an antiderivative, the definite integral from a to b equals F at b minus F at a: final value minus initial value.
groups.caption: If f is continuous and F is its antiderivative, its integral from a to b is F(b) − F(a): final value minus initial value.
groups.reason: Keep stated physical units, sign convention, assumptions and worked values legible at narration speed.
